Observation can help you decide whether to make room, offer help, or change something nearby. Start by noticing When you are unsure what your child is interested in or how much help they need. Age, interest & context When you want to understand your baby’s sounds, movements, or interests. General guidance for observing your baby; it does not ask for a particular skill. Watch what your child reaches toward, returns to, or spends time exploring. Notice their expressions and sounds, and what happens around them. Try to describe these details before deciding what they mean. You can do this while you are already together. Written notes are one option; both books also make room for simply watching when your hands are full. Notice your own words and reactions, too. The books use observation to understand an individual child and respond to them, including stepping in when help or protection is needed. Both books pair growing participation with an adult who notices what help is needed and remains available. In the everyday When your child is interested in joining in or working something out. Age, interest & context Notice a small response or effort and the help your baby needs. Participation can be a response during care; it does not require doing a task alone. Look for the part your child is already trying to do. Leave room for that effort, and offer enough help for them to continue. The point is their participation, not finishing every part alone. During exploration, the books distinguish effort from discouraging frustration. They describe watching, offering help when it is needed, and making space for another attempt. Davies also describes days when time or patience runs short: the adult can explain that they are helping this time and leave another opportunity for later. Help remains part of the relationship. Understanding an upset child and protecting them or someone else can happen together. In the everyday When your child is upset about a boundary. Age, interest & context When a necessary boundary or care situation brings distress. The adult keeps things safe and responds to needs; this is not an expectation that a young baby can remember a rule. The books describe acknowledging the feeling and remaining available, rather than trying to make every difficult feeling disappear. They also keep the adult responsible for stopping unsafe actions and showing what is acceptable. A child’s disappointment does not make the boundary unkind. The books describe useful surroundings that change with family life, without requiring a collection of special furniture or toys. In the everyday When setting up the home starts to feel like another large project. Age, interest & context When considering a change to your home. General guidance for the home you share with your baby. Look at what is helping and what is making everyday life harder. A useful change might make something easier to find, reduce repeated tidying, or give an interested child more room to take part. The Baby authors say Montessori can be practiced without buying special materials. Davies describes homes that retain their character, cultures, and traditions, including when space is shared or small. People belong to this environment too: their presence, language, and relationships matter alongside the physical space. What’s underneath The surroundings serve the child and the people who live there. Their visual mobiles are fragile and meant for looking; reaching and batting call for a different kind of material. In the everyday Your baby is interested in watching a slow movement or a changing view. Age, interest & context In the book: Early weeks and first 3 months; appendix examples also include around 3+ months. Interested in looking; reaching and batting call for tactile materials instead. The book’s examples have different ages. Interest and the kind of interaction matter more than completing a mobile sequence. The book’s examples include black-and-white shapes, reflective colored octahedrons, shades of one color, and paper figures that seem to dance. The authors also welcome other simple mobiles; the examples are not a set a family needs to acquire. They place visual mobiles in the awake movement area, separate from the bed. Looking at the mobile from underneath helps an adult consider the baby’s view. They favor gentle movement from air currents and do not require accompanying music. The authors watch for interest rather than a set viewing time. If the baby looks away, becomes tense or cries, they describe moving the mobile away, changing its position or trying another day. When reaching and batting begin, they distinguish sturdy tactile materials from these fragile looking mobiles. surfaces.entryText: small beginnings A Montessori companion All studies → A home within reach Your child’s age 0–3 months 3–6 months 6–9 months 9–12 months 12–18 months 18–24 months 2–3 years ← Three starting ideas A perspective Clothes that let your baby move The authors favor soft, comfortable clothes that let a baby move easily. They look for an easy opening for dressing and a fit that is neither tight nor so loose that it creases or tangles. In the everyday You are choosing everyday clothes or noticing how an outfit feels as your baby moves. Age, interest & context Choose with your baby’s current movements and comfort in mind. Wrap tops or a wider shoulder opening are among their examples. Their concern is how the clothes feel against the baby’s skin and how easily the adult can dress them. They prefer simple clothing with few hard fastenings or decorations. Separate tops and trousers, with socks if needed, are examples they give for freer movement. These are the authors’ clothing preferences, with comfort and movement at the center. Dressing itself can remain a gentle exchange with the baby. Sometimes play comes before a feed, and travel or changes at home can shift what is familiar. A repeated phrase or song can signal what is coming. The authors suggest coordinating with other caregivers where possible, while keeping the baby’s own cues in view. Family rituals can be part of that familiar world too: a regular park visit, a special breakfast or a celebration from one or more family cultures. The baby can be included before they can contribute much themselves. A short familiar routine can offer connection; falling asleep is not a performance. In the everyday Your baby is winding down or needs support settling. A few familiar words, a song or a short book are among the connecting moments they describe. The adult notices and responds, while the baby is the one who falls asleep. They describe gradually changing help when both baby and adult are ready, and explicitly say it is okay if feeding or rocking is currently part of settling. Their broader discussion also acknowledges night waking during the first year. The book’s sleep-surface recommendations contain tensions with its own safety box; this account concerns responsive support and does not choose a sleeping arrangement. Their position is not an absolute ban. In the everyday You are reading about pacifiers in the Montessori approach. Trying to understand the need goes alongside care, not ahead of needed help. In the everyday Your baby is crying and you are trying to understand what they need. They describe acknowledging a cry and responding with presence or holding when needed. Feelings can be heard without asking the baby to stop crying or insisting that everything is fine. Crawling and pulling-up examples apply when those movements begin. Their “yes space,” a term they credit to Magda Gerber and RIE, is an area prepared around what the baby can actually do. If your baby seems to want to keep playing, you can explain that wish to the other child. In the everyday Two children want the same object. Age, interest & context When your baby is holding something another child wants. Understanding sharing is not expected. The authors notice that a young baby may happily move to something else, or may want to hold on. Respond to what is happening rather than requiring either reaction. When your baby reaches for another child’s object, the book models asking whether that child is finished. Waiting, watching or finding another object are possibilities while the turn continues.
